requirements.requirement: Configure node1, node2, node3 as a three-member MariaDB Galera cluster
requirements.summary: All three nodes independently report wsrep_cluster_size=3, wsrep_cluster_status=Primary, and wsrep_local_state_comment=Synced after node1 bootstrapped via galera_new_cluster and node2/node3 joined via gcomm.

requirements.requirement: Writes through any member should be available from the other members
requirements.summary: A write on node1 was observed on node2 and node3; a subsequent write on node2 was observed on node3; a write on node3 was observed back on node1 — demonstrating full cross-node write propagation in both directions.

requirements.requirement: Keep the database available when one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: node2's mariadb was stopped; node1 immediately showed cluster size 2 / Primary and accepted a new write, which was confirmed visible on node3 while node2 remained down. This is a direct, bounded disruption test with observed availability.

requirements.requirement: Resynchronize an unavailable member automatically when it returns
requirements.summary: After node2's mariadb service was restarted (only systemctl start, no manual SST/join commands), it automatically rejoined the cluster via the configured gcomm address, and its own query showed cluster size 3, Synced, and all 4 rows including the one written during its downtime.

overall_summary: The executor built a functioning 3-node MariaDB Galera cluster and directly demonstrated all three material behavioral requirements: multi-master write propagation across all nodes, continued write availability with one member down (cluster size 2, Primary), and automatic rejoin/resync of the downed member with full data consistency restored. The independent node-restart protocol was also executed cleanly and sequentially on all three nodes, with boot-identity changes cross-confirmed against the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot, and cluster/data recovery verified after each reboot. The main blemish is an unremoved broad-privilege test database account left on the cluster after verification.
limitations: No SELinux AVC denial log or negative test (e.g., without the mysql_connect_any boolean) was captured, so the causal necessity of that specific SELinux change is inferred rather than directly proven, though it does not affect the observed successful outcome.
The task instruction does not specify a minimum outage/rejoin duration; the demonstrated outage window was short, so long-running or repeated failure/rejoin cycles were not exercised.

The 9 non-zero-exit commands in the trace correspond to expected transient states (SSH disconnects during reboot polling, systemctl is-active reporting 'inactive', and pre-install package checks finding nothing) rather than genuine failures, and were treated accordingly.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor mutations map directly to the task or the restart protocol (package installs, firewall/SELinux changes needed for Galera SST and replication traffic, galera.cnf writes, test schema for verification). However, the executor left a lingering 'galtest'@'%' MySQL account with ALL PRIVILEGES on *.* (created in cmd-17846a60fcde4539) that was never dropped after verification concluded — a retained, broad-privilege, remotely-accessible credential that was not cleaned up, a modest but real security-relevant residue. The password itself was generated with openssl and stored root-only (chmod 600) in cmd-94e0307af40647f0, which mitigates but does not eliminate the exposure. Additionally, benign temp files (/tmp/install.log, /tmp/install.pid, /tmp/mdb_start.log, /tmp/reboot.log) were left on all three nodes per the after-executor snapshot; these are low-risk, expected artifacts of install/reboot commands and not independently concerning. No failed services, no damaged package state, and firewall/SELinux changes were narrowly scoped to Galera's required ports/booleans.
